extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent applicants and practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patent obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103, including what prior art may be relied upon, how to treat analogous art, how to evaluate differences between prior art and the claimed invention, and how to handle applicant replies and rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness (KSR list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplary rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include: (A) Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way; (D) Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'Obvious to try' – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art; (G) Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2143 for discussion and examples illustrating use of these rationales to support an obviousness finding; examiners must articulate factual findings supporting the chosen rationale(s) rather than rely on conclusory statements (citing KSR, 550 U.S. at 418).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action; the reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant disagrees with factual findings, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred substantively; mere assertions that the Office failed to establish a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence are not substantively adequate under 37 CFR 1.111(b). Examiners may repeat the rejection and make the next Office action final if the traverse is ineffective (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must articulate findings of fact to support obviousness conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Office action should clearly communicate the Office’s findings and conclusions, articulating how the conclusions are supported by the findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making an obviousness rejection, examiners must set forth factual findings (Graham factors) and explain the rationale linking those facts to the legal conclusion of obviousness; follow procedures in MPEP §706.07(a) regarding finality of actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence (including secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence timely presented by applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination. Rebuttal evidence may include 'secondary considerations' such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may submit evidence to rebut factual findings (e.g., showing technological difficulties preventing combination, showing elements in combination do more than perform separate functions, or showing unexpected results). After rebuttal, examiners should reconsider the initial determination in view of the entire record and review all rejections and proposed rejections for continued viability. See MPEP §2145 and §§716–716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used in 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Before answering Graham’s 'content' inquiry, it must be known whether a patent or publication is in the prior art under 35 U.S.C. §102; subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. §102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103. Admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 103 rejection is based on appropriate 102 categories depending on the type and date of the reference. For overcoming certain references (e.g., publications), applicants may swear behind the reference under 37 CFR 1.131. See MPEP §§901–901.06(d), §§2121–2129, and §§2151–2155 for overview of prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content of the prior art (what the reference must disclose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations include availability of inoperative devices, the extent to which prior art must be enabling, whether broad disclosure rather than preferred embodiments suffices, and the effect of admissions in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§2121–2129 for case law on enabling disclosure, inoperative disclosures, and admissions as prior art; examiners must analyze the substantive teachings of the reference, not just bibliographic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine prior art content as of the time the invention was made to avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art must be determined 'at the time the invention was made' to avoid impermissible hindsight; decisionmakers should 'cast the mind back to the time the invention was made' and view the art as of that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using knowledge of the claimed invention to reshape the perceived problem or to make otherwise non-obvious combinations appear obvious; see MPEP §2145 subsection X.A for discussion of rebutting hindsight-based arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden and evidence to show benefits apply
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants the benefits of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) must establish that subject matter (only qualifying as prior art under subsections (e), (f) or (g) of pre-AIA §102) used in a §103 rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avail joint research agreement benefits, the applicant bears the burden to show (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) the invention resulted from activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) for requirements to establish common ownership/JRA. Historical limitations apply for certain filing/grant dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103 it must be analogous prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference must be analogous art to the claimed invention to be proper for use in an obviousness rejection. A reference is analogous if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing 'reasonably pertinent,' the reference must 'logically have commended itself to an inventor's attention' (In re Icon Health & Fitness) and examiners should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification. To support analogy, it may be appropriate to state the examiner's understanding of the problem and factual reasons why the prior art is pertinent. See In re Bigio, In re Klein, and In re Clay for related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant arguments on nonanalogous art should be evaluated against the specification and ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant argues the examiner misconstrued the problem and therefore relied on nonanalogous art, the examiner should fully consider the argument in light of the specification and the inferences a person of ordinary skill would draw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should use teachings of the specification to understand the problem to be solved and explain why an inventor would have looked to the cited reference; make factual findings supporting analogy determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider similarities and differences in structure and function when assessing analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarities and differences in structure and function between the prior art and the claimed invention carry greater weight than classification or cross-references when determining whether art is analogous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office classifications and search notes are evidence but structural/functional comparisons are more persuasive (citing In re Ellis). Examiners should emphasize structure/function parallels in rationale for relying on a reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous-art application across technical disciplines (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The analogous art test has been applied in chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts with discipline-specific considerations and precedent (examples provided: Ex parte Bland; Stratoflex; In re Mlot-Fijalkowski; Stevenson v. Int'l Trade Comm.; Medtronic v. Cardiac Pacemakers; In re Rosen; Ex parte Pappas; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate that: (a) problem similarity can make arts analogous across materials (chemical/dye arts); (b) similar structure/function in mechanical arts allows cross-field reliance; (c) designers may look to other product designs if the use/knowledge domain overlaps; (d) rate-limiting/electrical solutions can be analogous where the same technical problem exists. Use these precedents to inform factual analogy determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and claimed invention — consider the claimed invention 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining differences between the prior art and the claims at issue under 35 U.S.C. 103, the question is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim language and consider both the invention and the prior art references as a whole. Do not isolate single differences if the combination of elements as a whole provides nonobvious features (citing Stratoflex, In re Hirao).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust'—respect 'as a whole' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' of an invention disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid restricting analysis to a single perceived advantage or concept while ignoring express claim limitations; case law (e.g., W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb) shows courts reverse when the 'gist' approach disregards claim limitations or treats claims as though they read differently than allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of the source/cause of a problem can be a patentable contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable invention may lie in the discovery of the source of a problem even though the remedy may be obvious once the source is identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the inventive insight identifies an unexpected root cause (even if a known technique would then solve it), examiners must consider that insight as part of the 'as a whole' inquiry and assess obviousness accordingly.
